title: The debate
hookLine: the Samye debate: Kamalashila's gradual path against a Chan teacher's sudden path, as the Tibetan accounts tell it

cards: Two teachers in Tibet are saying different things about how awakening happens, and the king has to decide which way his monasteries will go.
One, a Chan master from China, teaches that awakening is sudden: stop grasping at thoughts and see your own nature directly.
The other, Kamalashila, an Indian scholar and a student of the abbot Shantarakshita, teaches that it comes step by step: ethics, study, careful reflection, meditation.
So, as the Tibetan accounts tell it, the king calls them to debate.

teach.b: Tibetans remember the Chinese master as Hashang Mahayana. In the accounts, he argues that any thought, good or bad, clouds the mind's clear nature, the way white clouds and black clouds alike hide the sun.
So stop chasing thoughts, stop grasping, and the sun is already there. Kamalashila answers: if you stop all thinking, how will you ever see clearly? Wisdom needs careful reflection.
Not-thinking alone is only a blank. He lays out stages, each resting on the one before, and tradition says he wrote them down in his Stages of Meditation.
In the Tibetan accounts, Kamalashila wins, and the king rules that Tibet will follow the gradual path of the Indian teachers. But be careful with the scoreboard.

This version comes to us from one side. Records from the Chinese side tell it differently, and historians ask whether it was a single debate at all or a longer exchange. And the sudden teaching didn't vanish.
It came up in Korea earlier on this road, when Chinul said awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually.
Chan and Zen schools carry the sudden way still, and Tibetan traditions later taught their own direct ways of looking at the nature of mind.
So one fair way to hear the debate is as two real insights pressing against each other.
Sudden: the sun was never gone. Gradual: the clouds still need clearing.

how: Debate is part of training in Tibetan monasteries, where monks question each other in courtyards with set gestures and a clap of the hands, and students study Kamalashila's Stages of Meditation.

o: a quarrel over who would rule Tibet next
a contest over sudden versus gradual awakening
an argument over which language to translate

s: every account agrees on who won
the Tibetan accounts say Kamalashila; other records, from the Chinese side, tell it differently.
in the accounts, the Chan master says even good thoughts cloud the mind
white clouds and black clouds alike hide the sun.
after the debate, the sudden teaching disappeared
Chan and Zen schools carry it still, and Chinul joined sudden and gradual in Korea.

games.q: you're the king of Tibet. two respected teachers disagree about how awakening happens. what do you do?
o: call them to debate in front of you.
games.why: as the Tibetan accounts tell it, the king called a debate and ruled for Kamalashila's gradual path.

practice: For the first half of the sit, try the sudden way: let every thought, pleasant or not, pass like clouds crossing the sky, without grabbing it.
For the second half, try the gradual way: turn one thought, about kindness or about change, over carefully. Notice what each is like from the inside, without deciding which is right.

wordCard.voice: The debate. At Samye, as the Tibetan accounts tell it, Kamalashila's gradual path met a Chan master's sudden path, and the king chose.

carryVoice: Your line: gradual and sudden. One side's scoreboard isn't the whole story. Until tomorrow.
